newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY'S GKI SEES LARGER GDP AND TRADE GAP IN '97.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY'S GKI SEES LARGER GDP AND TRADE GAP IN '97.

text.p: Hungary's investments, domestic demand and gross domestic product (GDP) are likely to turn to growth this year, slightly increasing the foreign trade deficit, GKI Economic Research said on Wednesday.

Last year's substantial cuts in the current account and budget deficits created the fundaments of growth, but policy-makers have to prevent an unjustified increase of household consumption in 1997, GKI said.
"GKI supposes that the deficits will widen slightly in line with economic growth," GKI Managing Director Andras Vertes told a news conference.

"If imports increase quickly in the interest of investments and modernisation, that's good," he said. "But a substantial rise in consumption would be unfavourable and jeopardise the results of economic stabilisation."
GKI said a rise was proable of one or two percent in household consumption in 1997, compared with an estimated three percent drop in 1996, and a government target of up to 0.5 percent for 1997.

Gross wages were likely to rise by some 21 percent, net wages by 22 to 23 percent, while tax changes would help real wages to increase by up to three percent, compared with a five percent fall last year, GKI added.

GKI said investments, which dropped by an estimated three percent in 1996, would grow by 10 percent this year, boosted by the increasing activity of the state and mainly those domestic companies which plan to boost their exports.
Increasing consumption and investments are likely to help the GDP to grow by 2.5 percent in 1997, after stagnation in 1996, GKI said.

Exports are likely to increase by 10 percent, compared with 13 percent last year, while imports would rise by 11 percent after 12 percent in 1996, boosting the foreign trade deficit by $400 to $500 million, to between $3 and $3.2 billion, GKI said.
However, the government should not allow the deficit to widen by more than that, and larger imports should serve the modernisation of the economy, GKI warned.
Vertes said Hungarian companies needed investments to improve their competitiveness, which will be weakened by the trade and monetary policy measures planned for this year.
Hungary plans to phase out its four percent import surcharge by July, increasing competition on the domestic market with imported products.
The monthly devaluation rate will be reduced to 1.1 percent on April 1 from 1.2 percent, and the government said it may further cut the rate in July.
However, a cut is not likely until September or October, and the reduction will not be larger than 10 basis points, Vertes said.
